body_markdown:
Heart failure has traditionally been viewed as a health condition that primarily affects older adults. However, new findings suggest that this perception may no longer reflect what is happening across the United States.


A recent report from the Heart Failure Society of America (HFSA) highlights a concerning increase in heart failure deaths, particularly among younger and middle-aged adults. The findings indicate that heart failure is becoming a growing public health concern across a much broader age range.


The report, published in the *Journal of Cardiac Failure* on October 5, 2026, examined trends in heart failure and associated deaths in the United States. Researchers found that deaths linked to heart failure increased substantially over the past decade, with younger adults experiencing some of the sharpest increases.


## Heart Failure Deaths Are Rising


According to the report, deaths associated with heart failure increased by 37% between 2010 and 2023. This represents a reversal of earlier progress in reducing heart failure mortality.


The increase is particularly striking among adults who are not traditionally considered to be in the highest-risk age group.


Among adults between 25 and 44 years old, heart failure deaths increased by 121% between 2010 and 2020. Adults aged 45 to 64 experienced a 96% increase during the same period.


For comparison, deaths among adults aged 65 and older increased by approximately 23%.


These figures do not necessarily mean that younger people have a higher overall risk of heart failure than older adults. Older adults continue to represent a major proportion of people affected by the condition. Instead, the figures show that heart failure is becoming increasingly important among younger populations.


## What Is Heart Failure?


Heart failure does not mean that the heart has completely stopped working. Instead, it describes a condition in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs.


When the heart's pumping ability becomes impaired, the body may not receive enough oxygen and nutrients. Fluid can also build up in the lungs and other parts of the body.


Symptoms can vary from person to person. Common warning signs include shortness of breath, persistent tiredness, swelling in the legs or ankles, difficulty exercising, rapid weight gain caused by fluid retention, and problems breathing when lying down.


Because some of these symptoms can develop gradually, people may mistake them for normal signs of aging, stress, being out of shape, or other health problems.


Recognizing persistent or worsening symptoms and discussing them with a healthcare professional can be important.


## Why Are Younger Adults Being Affected?


The growing burden of heart failure among younger Americans appears to be connected to the increasing prevalence of several conditions that can damage the cardiovascular system.


High blood pressure, obesity and diabetes are among the major risk factors highlighted in the report.


The report estimates that approximately one in three people with heart failure also have high blood pressure. A similar proportion have obesity, while about two in five have diabetes.


These conditions can place additional stress on the heart over time.


High blood pressure, for example, can force the heart to work harder to circulate blood. Persistent strain may eventually contribute to structural and functional changes in the heart.


Diabetes and obesity can also increase cardiovascular risk through several mechanisms, including metabolic changes, inflammation and damage to blood vessels.


The increasing occurrence of these chronic conditions among younger adults may therefore be contributing to heart failure becoming more common at earlier ages.


## A Significant Racial and Geographic Difference


The report also identifies important differences in heart failure rates across racial and geographic groups.


Black Americans were reported to have the highest rates of heart failure, with rates substantially higher than those reported among Asian Americans and white Americans.


Researchers also identified geographic patterns. States across the Deep South, Appalachia and the lower Midwest had some of the highest heart failure rates.


Mississippi, Oklahoma, Alabama and Arkansas were repeatedly among the states with the highest rates of heart failure deaths.


These differences can reflect a combination of factors, including rates of high blood pressure, diabetes and obesity, access to healthcare, socioeconomic conditions, environmental influences and differences in preventive care.


Understanding these disparities is important because effective heart failure prevention requires more than treating the disease after it develops. Public health efforts also need to address the conditions and circumstances that increase cardiovascular risk.


## Millions Could Face Heart Failure Risk


The report presents another important statistic: approximately one in four Americans could develop heart failure during their lifetime.


At present, roughly one-third of U.S. adults are considered to be at risk.


These numbers demonstrate why heart health cannot be viewed solely as an issue for older people.


Maintaining healthy blood pressure, managing blood sugar, achieving a healthy weight, staying physically active, avoiding tobacco and following appropriate medical treatment can all play a role in reducing cardiovascular risk.


Regular health checkups can also help identify problems before they become more serious. High blood pressure and diabetes, for example, can exist for years without causing obvious symptoms.


## The Economic Impact Could Also Grow


The consequences of rising heart failure rates extend beyond individual health.


Heart failure can require repeated medical appointments, medications, hospital stays, diagnostic testing and long-term care. As more people develop the condition, the financial pressure on patients, families and healthcare systems can increase.


The report estimates that the economic burden of heart failure in the United States could rise dramatically, from approximately $312 billion to $858 billion by 2050.


Such projections highlight the importance of prevention and early intervention.


Reducing the number of people who develop heart failure could potentially improve quality of life while also reducing healthcare costs.


## Prevention and Early Detection Matter


The new findings do not mean that heart failure is inevitable, particularly for younger adults.


Many of the health conditions associated with heart failure can be prevented, controlled or treated. Taking cardiovascular health seriously earlier in life may help reduce future risk.


People should pay attention to persistent symptoms such as unexplained breathlessness, unusual fatigue, swelling or sudden changes in weight. Anyone experiencing concerning or rapidly worsening symptoms should seek medical advice.


Healthcare professionals can also assess individual risk based on factors such as blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol, weight, family history and existing cardiovascular disease.


The broader message from the latest report is clear: heart failure is no longer an issue that can be considered exclusively a disease of old age.


The sharp rise in deaths among younger and middle-aged adults underscores the need for stronger prevention, earlier recognition and better access to effective treatment.


As heart failure continues to place a growing burden on Americans, improving cardiovascular health earlier in life could become increasingly important.
